title: US Utilities Join Trump Pledge to Shield Consumers From AI Power Costs
excerpt: Nearly 200 entities covering 80% of U.S. power delivery have signed on, as Congress advances the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act to prevent data center energy costs from reaching household bills.
body:
• Nearly 200 utilities and data center developers — including NextEra Energy, Duke Energy and Digital Realty — have signed Trump's pledge to prevent AI energy consumption from raising consumer electricity bills, covering about 80% of all U.S. power delivery.
  • The House Energy and Commerce Committee unanimously advanced the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act, requiring data centers consuming over 100 megawatts to cover costs of grid upgrades and new infrastructure.
  • Data centers are projected to consume 20% of U.S. electricity by 2035, up from 5.9% today, with Bank of America forecasting a 100-plus GW capacity gap through 2030.
  • Seven in ten Americans oppose data centers in their communities, driving bipartisan political action at federal and state levels.

The nation's largest utilities and data center developers have signed on to President Trump's pledge to pay more for the electricity needed to run AI models, in the White House's broadest effort yet to contain a backlash that has fueled protests and legislative proposals to halt the AI boom, according to the Wall Street Journal.

NextEra Energy, Duke Energy, Equinix and Digital Realty are among the nearly 200 entities committing to the promise that AI energy consumption will not push up bills for ordinary consumers. Republican governors including Louisiana's Jeff Landry and Georgia's Brian Kemp have also signed on. Trump is expected to announce the expanded commitments at a Thursday event at the Environmental Protection Agency.

The pledge now covers roughly 80% of all power delivered to U.S. homes and businesses, a White House official told the Journal. Commitments include paying for grid upgrades, negotiating separate rate structures with utilities and coordinating with grid operators to prevent blackouts.

A Widening Power Gap

The pledges arrive against a stark backdrop. Data centers are on track to consume about 20% of all U.S. electricity by 2035, up from 5.9% today, according to BloombergNEF. Bank of America analysts forecast the country will need more than 230 GW of new generating capacity over the next five years, but regulated utilities plan to add only about 93 GW — leaving a gap of more than 100 GW, according to Utility Dive.

Data centers alone could add roughly 125 GW of new electric load through 2030, pushing demand growth to a 4.1% compound annual rate and ending a decade of flat consumption. Large gas turbines are largely sold out through 2030, forcing developers toward on-site gas engines and battery storage.

"The market is no longer constrained by demand — it is constrained by where power can actually be delivered."

— Bank of America analysts, Global Research Report

Congress Moves to Codify Protections

While the White House pledge remains voluntary, Congress is moving to put similar protections into law. The House Energy and Commerce Committee on Tuesday unanimously advanced the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bipartisan bill by Rep. Gabe Evans (R-CO) and Rep. Kathy Castor (D-FL). The legislation would require state regulators to set standards for data centers consuming over 100 megawatts to cover the full costs of new generation, transmission and infrastructure upgrades.

Sen. Jon Husted (R-OH) introduced a companion bill in the Senate on Monday. "We have to build the energy infrastructure to support AI," Husted said. "But we must do that without passing the costs on to working families and small businesses."

Democrats have pushed for broader measures. Rep. Diana DeGette (D-CO) argued the bill fails to address data center water consumption — large facilities can use an estimated 5 million gallons per day. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have separately called for national moratoriums on new data center construction.

Public Anger Crosses Party Lines

The political urgency reflects deep public unease. A Gallup poll found seven in ten Americans would oppose an AI data center opening in their community. A separate Reuters/Ipsos survey found only 14% of respondents would support one being built in their area.

"When you read a quote about data centers, you don't know if it's Steve Bannon or Bernie Sanders speaking, which sums up the whole thing for me."

— Morgan Scarboro, Vice President, MultiState

At least 23 states have signed onto the White House pledge, and state legislatures are pursuing their own measures — from "pay your way" laws requiring hyperscalers to fund grid expansions to mandated reporting of water and electricity use.

Looking Ahead

For Indian Americans in tech hubs like Virginia, Texas and the Pacific Northwest, the debate cuts both ways: rising electricity costs affect household budgets, while regulatory slowdowns on data centers could ripple through AI hiring pipelines that sustain many H-1B and green card holders.

The pledges could prove difficult to enforce, since power prices are ultimately decided by state regulators. But the combination of the White House framework, the Ratepayer Protection Act and state-level action represents the strongest coordinated push yet to prevent AI's energy appetite from landing on ordinary ratepayers. Whether voluntary pledges and bipartisan legislation can keep pace with both AI's power demands and the public anger they have ignited remains an open question.
